title: Connection limits and pooling (the PgBouncer concept); shared_buffers and work_mem basics
summary: Connections are processes and their number is fixed at server start; memory is one shared cache sized at start plus per-operation budgets that multiply under load. Pool connections, keep work_mem modest and raise it per transaction, and know what a pooler does to session state.

examples.title: The first knobs: who can change them, and when it takes effect

annotations.note: context is the column to read first. postmaster: set at server start, a change needs a restart. superuser: a superuser (or a role granted SET on it) may change it per session. user: any session may change it for itself. The built-in defaults: shared_buffers 16384 pages of 8kB = 128MB, effective_cache_size 4GB, work_mem 4MB, maintenance_work_mem 64MB, 100 connections of which 3 are kept for superusers. initdb may write lower values into postgresql.conf if the machine can't support these.
work_mem is a per-operation budget, so raising it for one heavy transaction is safe and normal. SET LOCAL ends with the transaction; a plain SET would stay with the connection.

A session that sits idle inside an open transaction for 30 seconds is terminated. Such sessions hold their locks and stop VACUUM from removing dead rows; this timeout is the server-side guard against a client that forgot to commit. Set it per role rather than globally.

SQLSTATE 55P02. shared_buffers is one shared memory area allocated at start, and max_connections sizes shared structures too, which is why both need a restart. Plan them; you can't tune them on the fly.

examples.title: work_mem decides whether a sort spills to disk

annotations.note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query, and FORMAT JSON returns the plan as data, so the helper can return only the facts that are the same on every machine: the sort method and where it ran. The query text is spliced into SQL: fine for a lesson helper, never for user input.

external merge on Disk: the sort didn't fit in the default 4MB, so it wrote sorted runs to temporary files and merged them. Not an error, only slower; it shows up as temp_files in pg_stat_database and, with log_temp_files set, in the server log.
quicksort in Memory: 8MB is enough. In production this is the knob for one report or batch job, raised with SET LOCAL in its own transaction.
top-N heapsort keeps only the best 20 rows in a heap: 27kB, whatever the table's size. A missing LIMIT, or a missing index that would deliver the order, is often the real reason a sort spills.

examples.title: Session state, and what a pooler must reset between clients

annotations.note: Six kinds of session state: a setting, a custom variable, a prepared statement, a temporary table, a session-level advisory lock and a LISTEN. All of them belong to the server session, not to the client code that created them.
Everything is still there. A pool that hands this server session to another client as it is gives that client 256MB of work_mem, tenant 1 (the leak from the RLS lesson) and a lock it never took.

DISCARD ALL bundles RESET ALL, DEALLOCATE ALL, UNLISTEN *, pg_advisory_unlock_all(), DISCARD TEMP and a few more, and can't run inside a transaction block. It also reset this sandbox's own search_path, which is why the script only reads after it.
A clean session. The price is that the next client starts cold: no prepared statements, no cached plans. That is the trade PgBouncer's session mode makes on every client switch.

use_cases: Sizing max_connections and per-process pools for a service with several replicas, a worker, and cron jobs on one server
Putting PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of many short-lived clients (serverless functions, dozens of small services) that would otherwise exhaust max_connections
Giving a nightly report or an index build more memory (SET LOCAL work_mem, maintenance_work_mem) without raising it for every session
Setting idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout per role so one stuck client can't hold locks indefinitely
strengths: Unlike a JVM heap, most memory is budgeted per operation: work_mem, hash_mem_multiplier and maintenance_work_mem can be raised for one transaction without a restart
Operations that exceed work_mem spill to temporary files and finish, slower but correct, instead of failing
A pooler such as PgBouncer lets thousands of client connections share a few dozen server processes, with no change to the SQL in transaction mode as long as no session features are used
pg_settings documents every knob's unit, default and context, so a configuration review is a query
weaknesses: Each connection is a server process: opening one is expensive, and max_connections, fixed at start, caps the whole server
work_mem is per sort or hash node per session, so the worst case is work_mem × nodes × sessions; there is no global cap
shared_buffers and max_connections need a restart, so getting them wrong costs a maintenance window
Transaction pooling breaks session features (SET, PREPARE, session advisory locks, LISTEN, WITH HOLD cursors, temp tables that outlive a transaction) silently rather than with an error

pitfalls.title: Raising max_connections instead of pooling
pitfalls.detail: More connections than the server has CPUs and disks to serve add contention, not throughput, and every slot sizes shared memory. Keep max_connections modest, size each process's pool from the budget (the pgx lesson does the arithmetic), and add PgBouncer when the number of client processes outgrows it.

pitfalls.title: A global work_mem raise
pitfalls.detail: A server-wide 256MB looks harmless until 100 sessions each run a query with three sort and hash nodes. Keep the global value small and raise it where a known heavy query runs.
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB'; -- the report; COMMIT;

pitfalls.title: Session features behind transaction pooling
pitfalls.detail: With PgBouncer in transaction mode, a SET, a PREPARE or a pg_advisory_lock() lands on whichever server session ran that transaction; your next transaction may get another one, and another client may inherit it. Use SET LOCAL or set_config(..., true), pg_advisory_xact_lock, and a direct connection for LISTEN.
pitfalls.bad: SET statement_timeout = '2s';  -- through a transaction-mode pooler
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '2s'; ...; COMMIT;  -- or ALTER ROLE tracelite_app SET statement_timeout = '2s'

pitfalls.title: Timeouts in postgresql.conf
pitfalls.detail: The docs advise against setting statement_timeout, lock_timeout or transaction_timeout in postgresql.conf, because they would hit every session, maintenance and migrations included. Set them per role or per transaction.

quiz.q: Which of these needs a server restart to change?
quiz.why: shared_buffers has context postmaster: the shared memory is allocated at start. The others have context user.

quiz.q: work_mem is 64MB and 50 sessions each run a query with two sorts and one hash join (hash_mem_multiplier 2.0). Roughly how much memory may those operations use at the same time?
quiz.why: Each sort may use work_mem and each hash work_mem × 2: (2 × 64 + 128) MB per session, times 50.

quiz.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE of a nightly report shows Sort Method: external merge. What's the first fix to try?
options: Raise work_mem in postgresql.conf for everyone
SET LOCAL work_mem for the report's transaction (or add a LIMIT or an index that delivers the order)
quiz.why: The spill is about one operation's budget. Raising it globally multiplies across every session; shared_buffers is a cache, not sort memory.

quiz.q: A Go service behind PgBouncer in transaction mode runs SET app.tenant = '7' and then its queries, each in its own transaction. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: PgBouncer replays SET for every transaction
The setting stays on the server session that ran it, so later transactions may miss it and other clients may inherit it
quiz.why: PgBouncer's docs list SET as unsupported in transaction pooling; only a handful of reported parameters are tracked. Use set_config(..., true) inside each transaction.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Resource Consumption (shared_buffers, work_mem, hash_mem_multiplier)
PostgreSQL docs: Client Connection Defaults (statement, lock and idle timeouts)
PostgreSQL docs: effective_cache_size and other planner settings

body:
## Concept

Two resources run out first, and both are fixed more rigidly than you might expect.

**Connections.** Every connection is a server process. `max_connections` (default 100)
is set at server start, and PostgreSQL sizes parts of its shared memory from it;
`superuser_reserved_connections` (3) and `reserved_connections` (0) are carved out of it.
Every replica's pool, every worker, migration job and psql session shares that budget.

**Memory** comes in two kinds:

- `shared_buffers` is the shared page cache, allocated once at start (default 128MB). On
  a dedicated server with 1GB or more of RAM the docs suggest starting at 25% of memory;
  beyond about 40% it rarely helps, because PostgreSQL also relies on the operating
  system's file cache. `effective_cache_size` only tells the planner how much cache to
  assume; it allocates nothing.
- `work_mem` (default 4MB) is the budget for **one** sort or hash operation before it
  spills to temporary files. A query can run several such operations at once, hashes get
  `work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier` (2.0), and every session has its own.
  `maintenance_work_mem` (64MB) does the same for `VACUUM`, `CREATE INDEX` and adding
  foreign keys.

A **connection pool** keeps a few connections open and lends them out. An application
pool (pgxpool) does that inside one process; a **pooler** such as PgBouncer sits between
many client connections and a few server connections, for all clients at once.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java:** HikariCP, Node's `pg.Pool`, `psycopg_pool` and pgxpool are all application
  pools. PgBouncer is the same idea moved out of process, so twenty service instances
  can share forty server connections instead of opening twenty pools of twenty.
- **Threads vs processes:** MySQL serves a connection with a thread; PostgreSQL starts a
  process for each one. Opening a connection is correspondingly expensive, which is why
  poolers are standard equipment rather than an optimisation.
- **Memory model:** `shared_buffers` behaves like a JVM heap fixed with `-Xms = -Xmx` at
  start; `work_mem` is closer to a per-request buffer limit in C, with a defined fallback
  (an external merge sort on disk) instead of an out-of-memory failure.

## How it works

The arithmetic to keep in mind:

- **Connections:** replicas × pool size + workers + jobs + admin sessions ≤
  `max_connections` − reserved slots. The `go.postgres.pgx` lesson works an example.
- **Memory:** `shared_buffers` + sessions × (sort/hash nodes per query × `work_mem`) +
  maintenance operations × `maintenance_work_mem`, plus the operating system's file
  cache, must fit in RAM. The per-session term is the one that surprises people.

PgBouncer has three pool modes
([features](https://www.pgbouncer.org/features.html),
[configuration](https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html)):

- **session** (the default): a client keeps one server connection until it disconnects;
  then PgBouncer runs `server_reset_query`, `DISCARD ALL` by default, before the next
  client gets it. Every feature works; you save connection setup, not connections.
- **transaction**: a client gets a server connection only for the duration of a
  transaction. The reset query is not used. Per the PgBouncer docs, `SET`/`RESET`,
  `LISTEN`, `PREPARE`/`DEALLOCATE`, `WITH HOLD` cursors, session-level advisory locks,
  `LOAD` and temp tables that outlive a transaction are not supported. Protocol-level
  prepared statements (the kind pgx uses) work when `max_prepared_statements` is
  non-zero.
- **statement**: transaction pooling that also forbids multi-statement transactions.

## Design notes

- **Pool in the process, and pool in front when processes multiply.** One pgxpool per
  process, sized from the server's budget. Add PgBouncer in transaction mode when the
  number of processes (replicas, serverless functions, many small services) makes the
  sum outgrow `max_connections`, and write the code for it from day one: transaction-
  scoped settings, `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, a direct connection for `LISTEN`.
- **Memory defaults to change on a real server:** `shared_buffers` toward 25% of RAM;
  `effective_cache_size` to what the OS will actually cache; `work_mem` modest globally
  and raised per transaction; `maintenance_work_mem` larger, since few maintenance
  operations run at once.
- **Timeouts per role:** `ALTER ROLE tracelite_app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
  = '60s'` and a `statement_timeout` suited to the service, not in postgresql.conf.
- **StackLab's runner** shows the other end of the spectrum. `sqlrun` opens one
  connection per run (two for multisession) and `runexec` closes it afterwards: no pool,
  so one learner's `SET`s, temp tables and locks can't reach the next run. This example's
  `DISCARD ALL` shows how much a pool would otherwise have to reset. Runs are short, at most two
  at a time (ADR-0008), and each one sets its own `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout`
  (`sandboxSQL` in `server/internal/sqlrun/sqlrun.go`): `SET LOCAL` for the
  transactional runtime, session-level for `sql-nontx`, where the connection is closed
  afterwards anyway.
